extracted.intended_audience: researchers, developers and advanced users of proof assistants and formal mathematical repositories (especially Mizar users and library maintainers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for designing, organizing, storing, reviewing, and evolving a large centrally-managed formal mathematical library (the Mizar Mathematical Library) to support reuse, verification, automation, and collaborative development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design goals of the Mizar language/system
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mizar language/system was designed so that (a) papers could be stored in a computer and later, at least partially, translated into natural languages, (b) the papers would be formal and concise, (c) it would form a basis for construction of an automated information system for mathematics, (d) it would facilitate detection of errors, verification of references, elimination of repeated theorems, etc., (e) it would open a way to machine assisted education of the art of proving theorems, (f) it would enable automated generation of input into typesetting systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These early design goals indicate the intended balance between human readability and machine checkability; design decisions and library policies should further these aims (readability, formal rigor, reusability, automation support, educational use, and typesetting integration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized, centrally-managed knowledge base
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision to build the Mizar Mathematical Library (MML) as a centrally-managed knowledge base maintained together with the formalization language and the verification system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A centrally-managed repository enables effective reuse of previously collected notions, consistent evolution of the language and verifier, and coordinated review/revision policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support efficient accumulation, maintenance and re-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale formalizations require developing methods of efficiently accumulating, maintaining and re-use of previously generated mathematical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Library infrastructure should avoid duplication, support selective import/export, and provide tools for locating and reusing existing facts instead of re-proving them ad hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal axiomatization principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid declaring ad-hoc axiomatics required for proving facts in each article; aim to establish 'a minimal axiomatization' for a particular article to reduce the risk of contradictory axioms and repetitions of already proved facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proving common properties from basic axioms rather than embedding extra axioms; restructure axiomatic files into minimal core plus derived, user-friendly formulations (as done with TARSKI_0, TARSKI_A, TARSKI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and management of global axiomatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide on the foundational axiomatization for the library (e.g., Tarski–Grothendieck set theory was chosen for the MML after experiments with other foundations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should consider compatibility with targeted formalizations (category theory, etc.), allow experiments but converge on a stable choice to ease reuse; if multiple axiomatizations are allowed, provide mechanisms to manage them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of article texts and exported abstracts (public interface)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors decide which definitions and statements to export; during peer review exportable items are selected and extracted to form the 'abstract', containing bare statements stripped of proofs. This public interface is stored in the database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a clear distinction between local/internal content and exported public interface; store only necessary formula/notation/type information for exported items to enable safe reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured semantic storage (constructors, vocabularies, formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Database stores for each definition/theorem/scheme/registration the corresponding formula represented using constructors; definitions include notation (format and type info), argument positions, arity, and result/mother types; symbols are grouped into vocabularies with possible priority declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design internal data formats (XML-based in MML) to capture semantic, syntactic, and presentation metadata to support unambiguous import, overloading resolution, and cross-verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Import/export directives and controlled importing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use designated Mizar directives (vocabularies, constructors, notations, registrations, requirements, expansions, equalities, etc.) to import only the necessary information; due to overloading the order of used notations is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide fine-grained import controls so authors can limit the amount of imported information and ensure processing time remains reasonable regardless of formalization complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use language-level automation features rather than hard-coded procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift the focus from implementing hard-coded system procedures toward language extensions like registrations, properties, or reductions to enable automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design language features that encode common automation patterns (e.g., registrations for term reductions) while keeping them expressible and reviewable in the library articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Configurable automation ('requirements')
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce configurable automation of commonly used notions (requirements) so users can decide whether certain facts (e.g. arithmetic facts) are treated as obvious by the checker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide justifications of automatically-obvious facts in ordinary articles to enable cross-verification and allow switching off automation for education or axiomatic experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Library organization and modular separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the library into modular parts (e.g., concrete vs abstract parts, SCM part, Addenda, EMM) to isolate frequently revised components and simplify browsing and reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group articles so that parts not depending on higher-level notions are processed first; isolate machine-modeling parts or frequently-changing modules to reduce cascading revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and review processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a reviewing process coordinated by a Library Committee with verdicts accept/revise/reject and an additional D (Delay) grade; revisions may be authored, automatic, pretty-printing, or reorganization-driven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reviewing and graded revision policies to keep the repository small, preserve clear organization, and encourage 'elegant' mathematics (short definitions, better proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Human supervision over automatic revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatic generalizations or automated dropping of assumptions can be dangerous (example: removing type assumptions may lead to nonsensical classifications like 'π is odd').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although automation improves the library, supervise automatic revisions carefully with human reviewers to avoid semantic regressions and unintended consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide and use tooling for search, duplication detection and authoring assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools like MML Query, Mizar Proof Advisor (a 'hammer' for MML), MoMM (Most of Mizar Matches), and fast matchers help fetch matching theorems and detect duplications; version-control systems (MML CVS) have limitations due to lack of stable absolute names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in robust tooling for querying, premise selection, duplication detection, and author assistance; be aware of version-control challenges and improve change traceability and item naming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain integrity and avoid contradictory axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ad-hoc or conflicting environment declarations by authors which could introduce contradictory items; the librarian/extractor/accommodator approach was introduced to avoid repeated ad-hoc axiomatics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce policies and tooling to detect contradictory axioms and ensure a minimal, consistent set of assumptions for each article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable naming and traceability of items
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no absolute names for MML items and massive changes can make it hard to find relevant modifications; this limits usefulness of some versioning tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt naming conventions and change-tracking mechanisms that provide human-readable and machine-usable identifiers to improve reviewability and history analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and analyze library metrics to guide development
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect metrics (e.g., number of constructors/notations, properties, registrations; ratio of theorems to definitions; theorem-dependence trees; author contributions, submission timelines) to understand library structure and development trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative analysis of dependencies and usage (information transfer measures, Shannon-based metrics) to identify hotspots, heavily-used articles, duplication, and to prioritize maintenance and tooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for human readability and mathematician-oriented vernacular
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mizar language was designed to be readable by mathematicians while being sufficiently rigorous for computer verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language and library conventions should favor readability by domain experts to encourage adoption, while preserving formal precision needed for machine checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export only necessary presentation and automation metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to formulas, the database should store presentation-related data (new notations, synonyms/antonyms for objects) and automation data (registrations, term reductions and identifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exported metadata should be rich enough to enable correct presentation and automation in importing articles but limited to what is needed to avoid bloat and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policies on allowing multiple axiomatizations and stored information
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming the library, address whether various axiomatizations should be allowed, how to build the knowledge database and what information should be stored, and how to organize, manage and ensure integrity of the database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish explicit policies on axiomatization permissibility, schema for stored items, and integrity checks to ensure long-term coherence of the repository.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage modular, reusable encodings of mathematical structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Retrospective introduction of common formal frameworks (e.g., hierarchies of Mizar structures) was used to gain better representation of ordinary mathematical practice and improve reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, refactor and generalize previously ad-hoc encodings into modular, hierarchical structures to reduce duplication and improve cross-domain reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance aggressive generalization with preservation of intended typing/semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatic generalization that removes type restrictions may lead to over-general facts that hold syntactically but are semantically meaningless; such automation must be balanced against preserving intended domain constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying automatic generalization, include safeguards (tests, human review, or provenance) that preserve meaningful type constraints and intended semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use abstracts (proof-stripped statements) for efficient reuse and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'abstract' extraction (bare statements without proofs) enables storing a public interface and optimizing import/export and database operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate and maintain concise proof-stripped abstracts for faster dependency analysis, import, and to decouple proof changes from interface stability where possible.
